newsitem.title: USA: For-profit, nonprofit hospitals not so different.
newsitem.headline: For-profit, nonprofit hospitals not so different.

text.p: Amid controversy about whether the spread of for-profit hospitals might limit access to quality care, a new study suggested Wednesday that the investor-owned hospitals might not be very different from nonprofits.
In the decade from 1986, 87 hospitals across the country converted from nonprofit to for-profit status. Other hospitals merged, and some were closed during the decade.
Health policy experts generally expect that trend to continue as hospitals struggle to survive in more competitive markets under cost-cutting pressures.

Reasons for controversy over conversions to for-profit status include concern about monopolies, fear that charity care to the uninsured will be cut, and worry that investor-owned hospitals or chains will place profits before patient care.

The new study, financed by the Federation of American Health Systems which represents for-profit hospitals, found that many of the deals were put together with little public input or regulatory oversight.
In some cases, hospital policies were being shaped by distant corporate headquarters, not in the local community.
Defenders say that the for-profit hospitals tend to be more efficient, pay taxes to the community, bring in capital to modernise and improve facilities, and may save ailing hospitals from closing.

The authors of the study said much more research was needed, particularly to assess the quality of health care, but they did not find any trends toward serious problems when hospitals become investor-owned.
"In and of itself, conversion doesn't cause problems," said Marc Berk, the project director.

Researcher Tami Mark of the independent Project Hope Centre for Health Affairs, which carried out the study, said that hospitals that allowed themselves to be acquired by for-profit companies tended to be in poor financial shape and facing "cost-cutting pressures from managed care companies, third party payors and public sector payors," such as Medicare.
After conversion, they tended to be in better financial shape. There was short-term evidence that levels of charity care and community services provided by the hospitals were similar.
The new study combined an analysis of nationwide data and 10 case studies.

Conversions can yield problems, Federation president Tom Scully acknowledged in a briefing. For instance, the study found that at Columbia/HCA Cedars Medical Centre in Miami, employee morale had worsened since the for-profit takeover.
"The results are a very mixed bag," Scully said. "But the differences between investor-owned and community-owned (hospitals) are vastly overblown."
